Debate persists about presidential removal power not only on the 
doctrinal level, but also with regard to what is at stake in practical terms. 
Limits on the removability of administrators are not necessarily a reliable 
measure of an agency’s effective political independence from the president. 
The president, for example, often need not remove officers in order 
ultimately to control the membership of independent agencies. Members of 
independent boards and commissions rarely serve their full terms. One 
study examined the history from 1945 to 1970 of seven important agencies, 
whose members were statutorily granted terms of office ranging from five 
to seven years. This era was marked by considerably less party polarization 
than Congress has witnessed in recent decades, so it is an open question 
whether its conclusions still hold. Nonetheless, during this earlier period, 
the president had only once needed more than three years to name an 
actual majority of the Commissioners, and the average timo from 
inauguration to appointment of a majority was twenty-one months. When 
the presidency changed parties, the average time for the president to gain 
a partisan majority on a Commission was but seven months. These figures 
illustrate that, even with limited removal authority, the president retains 
substantial power to shape the membership, and thus presumably the 
policies, of the independent agencies. Charles T. Goodsell & Ceferina C. 
Gayo, Appointive Control of Federal Regulatory Commissions, 23 Ad min . 
L. Re v . 291 (1971). On the reluctance of non-chair independent commission 
members to serve their full terms, see Brian D. Feinstein & David Zaring, 
Disappearing Commissioners, 109 IOWAL. Re v . 1041 (2024).
Independent agency statutes also typically permit the president to 
choose the agency’s chair; despite their coEegial design, the chair in many 
agencies has considerable control over the group’s agenda and may thus be 
weU positioned to align the agency’s policy output with the president’s 
platform. Todd PhiEips, Commission Chairs, 40 YALE J. Re g . 277 (2023). 
For skeptical assessments whether agency structural independence is a 
refiable predictor of agency cooperation with the president’s poEcy agenda, 
see Neal Devins & David E. Lewis, Not-So Independent Agencies: Party 
Polarization and The Limits of Institutional Design, 88 B.U. L. Re v . 459 
(2008); Symposium: The Independence of Independent Agencies, 1988 DUKE 
L.J. 215 (1988). See also Adrien Vermeule, Conventions of Agency 
Independence, 113 COLUM. L. Re v . 1163, 1165-1166 (2013) (arguing that 
the idea of “conventions”—regular patterns of poEtical behavior foEowed 
from a sense of obEgation even though not strictly required by law—is 
critical to understanding the degree of independence any agency enjoys).
